To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the sensitivity of prostate MRI is low in men with a clinically significant cancer and that focal therapy is not feasible in the majority of men with a clinically suspicious MRI lesion.
the use of the IMPROD biparametric magnetic resonance imaging (bp-MRI) protocol is feasible and can be used for focal therapy planning in men with a suspicion of PCa.

the use of IMPROD biparametric magnetic resonance imaging (bpMRI) in men with a suspicion of prostate cancer has a high sensitivity for detecting clinically significant prostate cancer (CS-PCa) in the whole prostate, and that the use of this imaging modality is feasible for focal therapy planning.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel imaging methods and their clinical implementation in the diagnosis, staging, and therapy planning of prostate cancer.
the development, validation and clinical application of novel MRI techniques for the detection and characterization of prostate cancer and their application for focal therapy.
the development and evaluation of new imaging methods for the diagnosis and therapy planning of PCa, with the aim of improving the treatment of patients with PCa and to reduce side effects.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no single imaging modality that is superior to another, and that the best approach is to use a multimodality imaging approach to maximize the diagnostic yield.
the current evidence is insufficient to determine whether prostate MRI has any impact on clinical decision‐making in men with a suspicion of PCa.

the use of MRI for prostate cancer diagnosis and staging is still in its infancy, and that the current literature is still insufficient for a conclusive statement on the value of MRI in the management of patients with PCa.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
MRI‐based focal therapy is feasible, and that the combination of MRI and biopsy is the most accurate way to identify the cancer in the prostate.
we have shown that the IMPROD method is a sensitive method for detection of prostate cancer in men with suspicion of prostate cancer, and that the method can be used in focal therapy planning.
the sensitivity of prostate MRI is high in men with a suspicion of PCa, especially in men with high-grade PCa.
The main takeaway from our work is that

focal therapy can be considered for men with a clinical indication for treatment and with a low‐risk prostate cancer on biopsy, if MRI‐based assessment of tumor volume and location is used to select patients and to plan focal treatment.

the IMPROD biparametric prostate MRI (bpMRI) protocol is a promising method for focal therapy planning, with high sensitivity and negative predictive value (NPV), and a low rate of missed cancers in the prostate.
the sensitivity of prostate MRI for PCa detection can be improved by using an MRI‐based segmentation method that takes into account the heterogeneity of PCa.
